items.title: #1 The Day Mirror 1 Arrived!
items.caption:
It was 29 October 2025

This was the day my first Magic Mirror arrived.

Gemma and I unpacked it and couldn’t wait to try it.

The mirror was exactly what I’d hoped for…

The software wasn’t.

It wasn’t terrible.

It just wasn’t really… anything.

And it definitely wasn’t me.

So I did what anyone would do.

I started searching online for another program.

Surely someone had already built exactly what I wanted?

I found lots of options.

Some looked okay.

But every one of them wanted another monthly subscription, and none of them felt quite right.

At the time I wasn’t thinking,

“I’m going to build my own software.”

I was thinking,

“There has to be something out there that does exactly what I want.”

I kept looking.

And looking.

Eventually I realised…

I was describing a product that didn’t seem to exist.

At some point I stopped searching for software…

…and started making a list of everything I wished it could do.

Then that list kept growing.

Not just with the things I wanted…

…but with ideas I didn’t even know I wanted in a photo booth.

I never planned to build software.

I never planned to build a website.

I definitely never planned to spend the next nine months learning things I’d never even heard of.

I just couldn’t settle for “good enough.”

One idea became another.

Then another.

Then another.

Until one day…

Instapic existed.

Today, exactly nine months later…

I’m proud.

Not because it’s finished…

(it probably never will be!)

But because an idea scribbled on a piece of paper somehow became something real.

Something that didn’t exist before.

And something that’s unmistakably me.

❤️ Lorie x
items.alt: Gemma and I posing together in front of our first Magic Mirror on the day it arrived.

items.title: #2 I Accidentally Built Something Else Today
items.caption:
I walked into my office this morning with absolutely no intention of building anything new.

I already had a list.

A sensible list.

Things to test.
Things to tidy.
Things I had already started.

Then I noticed one small thing missing from the Instapic website:

A gallery.

That should have been simple.

Just make a page, add a few photos and call it done… right?

Except a website gallery wasn’t enough.

Because I didn’t want to open website files, resize and move media, edit data by hand, remember which posts were drafts, then run Git commands every single time I wanted to add something new.

I wanted the gallery to work the way the rest of Instapic works:

From one place.
Under my control.
And connected properly to everything behind it.

So I built the public gallery.

It can display photo strips, individual photos, collages, GIFs, Boomerangs, videos and social posts. It sorts them into sections, keeps the portrait media looking like phone stories and lets visitors move through the moments without cluttering the homepage.

Then, naturally, I built the system behind the gallery too.

Inside my Instapic MotherPC Admin area, I can now:

• Upload media
• Create titles and captions
• Add image descriptions
• Choose content types and categories
• Arrange the display order
• Save unfinished ideas as private drafts
• Edit or delete posts
• Approve exactly what is allowed to appear publicly
• Publish the finished gallery directly to the live website

And because apparently even that wasn’t enough, pressing Publish does more than update a page.

It gathers only the approved content, prepares the website gallery, copies the correct media, records the change in Git and pushes a fresh backup to GitHub before it goes live.

The screenshot on the left is what everyone sees.

The screenshot on the right is the part I decided I also needed to build so I could create and publish it myself.

I didn’t just add a gallery to a website.

I built the content system that runs it.

I had absolutely no plan to do any of this when I walked into the office this morning.

I just thought:

“We’re probably missing a gallery.”

This keeps happening.

I notice one small thing.

Then I wonder if it could work a little better.

One idea becomes another.

Then another.

Then apparently I’ve built an entire gallery, content-management system and direct publishing pipeline before I’ve even had time to reconsider the original idea.

So yes—I accidentally built something else today.

I just didn’t know I was going to when I arrived.

❤️ Lorie x
items.alt: Side-by-side screenshots showing the live Instapic gallery and the MotherPC Gallery and Content publishing workspace used to manage it.

items.title: #3 I’m Glad I Didn’t Know AI Agents Existed
items.caption:
When I started building instapic, I didn’t even know connected AI coding agents existed.

I had ChatGPT & Grok.

I would explain what I wanted to build, & they would give me Bash commands or blocks of code.

Then I had to take those instructions to the terminal myself.

Open the terminal.

Type the command.

Find the file.

Open it in nano.

Work out where the new code belonged.

Paste it.

Save it.

Exit.

Restart the program.

Test it.

Then go back & explain what worked, what broke & what happened next.

At the time, I had no idea there would eventually be AI agents that could open files, navigate the project & make changes directly.

Honestly, I’m glad I didn’t know.

If I’d had that from the beginning, I might never have learnt what I did.

The manual process forced me to understand where every file lived, what each section controlled & how every hook connected to the next part of the system.

I had to know whether a change belonged in the booth, Mother PC, the website, a Python route, a JavaScript runtime, a service file or one of the growing collection of patches.

When something broke, I could usually remember where we had been, what we had changed & why two pieces were probably conflicting.

Not always immediately & definitely not without frustration.

But I wasn’t pressing a button & waiting for software to appear.

I was inside the build.

I saw every command.

I opened every file.

I followed every path.

I tested every connection.

I learnt how the whole system fitted together because I had no other way to build it.

Today, connected AI agents help me move faster. They inspect the project, trace problems & even work directly across the system.

But they’re working inside an architecture I already understand—because I built it the slow way first.

Would I want to go back to copying every Bash command, opening nano & closing it again thousands of times?

Absolutely not 😂

But I wouldn’t trade what that process taught me.

AI helped me work out how to build Instapic.

I was still the person at the terminal, making the decisions, performing the changes, testing every result & refusing to stop when it broke.

And I’m glad I learnt it that way.

❤️ Lorie x
